unit.unitOverview: Level 1 taught you to compare two things and name the best of several. This unit is about precision rather than comparison: the fixed order English uses when several adjectives stack up, the forms for describing how well something is done, and the class of adjectives that already mean extremely and therefore cannot be made stronger. It ends with two product descriptions of the same object, because precision is most visible where somebody is trying to avoid it.
unit.learningPath:

visual.lectureScript:
Three patterns, and the first is the strangest thing in this level: a rule that every English speaker follows exactly and almost none of them can state.
When you put several adjectives in front of a noun, they go in a fixed order.
A small round wooden table. Not a wooden round small table.
Both are grammatically parseable and only one sounds like English. Native speakers will tell you the second is wrong and will not be able to say why, because the order is learned by exposure and never taught.
The order is: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
A lovely little old rectangular brown Italian wooden dining table. That is all eight, and no real sentence ever uses all eight — three is common, four is a lot.
A useful way to hold it: the further from the noun, the more it is your view; the closer to the noun, the more it is a fact about the thing. Lovely is your opinion and goes first. Wooden is a fact and goes last, because in a sense wooden table is almost one word.
The practical version, since eight categories is too many to check in conversation: opinion first, material last, size before colour. That covers most real cases.
And one thing that lets you avoid the whole problem — and native speakers use it constantly. Do not stack more than two or three. Use a relative clause or a phrase instead. A small wooden table that we bought in Italy, rather than a small old Italian wooden table. Stacking four adjectives is grammatically fine and stylistically heavy, and breaking them up is usually better writing anyway.
Second pattern: comparative adverbs.
In Level 1 Unit 12 you learned adverbs of manner — quickly, carefully, well. Now the comparative and superlative of those.
The rule follows the adjectives from Unit 4, with one difference that catches people.
Most adverbs end in -ly, and -ly words are long, so they take more and the most. More carefully. More quickly. The most carefully.
But a small group of very common adverbs are short and take -er and -est, exactly like adjectives. Fast, faster, the fastest. Hard, harder, the hardest. Early, earlier, the earliest. Late, later, the latest.
And the two irregulars you already have: well, better, the best. Badly, worse, the worst.
So the error to avoid is more faster or more quicker on one side, and quicklier on the other. Long -ly adverbs take more. Short ones take -er. And well is better, never more well.
Third pattern, and this is the one that changes how you sound.
Some adjectives are gradable and some are not.
A gradable adjective can be more or less. Cold. You can be a bit cold, quite cold, very cold, extremely cold. It is a scale.
A non-gradable adjective is already at the end of its scale. Freezing does not mean cold — it means at the extreme of cold. You cannot be very freezing, because there is nowhere further to go.
The pairs matter: cold and freezing, hot and boiling, tired and exhausted, angry and furious, pleased and delighted, difficult and impossible, good and perfect, big and enormous, small and tiny, surprising and astonishing.
And here is the point: the two kinds take different degree words.
Gradable adjectives take very, quite, rather, extremely, a bit.
Non-gradable adjectives take absolutely, completely, utterly, totally, entirely.
Very cold. Absolutely freezing.
Very tired. Absolutely exhausted.
Very angry. Absolutely furious.
Saying very freezing is the single most recognisable non-native pattern in this whole area, and it is easy to fix, because there is a test. If the adjective already means extremely something, it is non-gradable, and it takes absolutely.
Two exceptions worth knowing. Really works with both — really cold and really freezing are both fine, which makes really the safe choice when you are unsure. And absolutely is used with a small number of gradable adjectives for emphasis, but you do not need to produce that; you only need to not be confused by it.
One last thing. Non-gradable adjectives are stronger, so they are used less often. A speaker who describes everything as absolutely exhausted and utterly furious has nowhere left to go, and the words stop meaning anything. Precision includes reserving the strong word for when it is true.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: The Rule Nobody Is Taught
readings.passageScript:
A small round wooden table.
A wooden round small table.
Every English speaker will tell you the second is wrong. Almost none of them can tell you why, because the order of adjectives is learned entirely by exposure and is never taught in school.
The order is: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.
A lovely little old rectangular brown Italian wooden dining table uses all eight, and no real sentence ever does. Three adjectives is common. Four is already heavy.
There is a way of holding the order that is easier than the list. The further an adjective sits from the noun, the more it is your view of the thing. The closer it sits, the more it is a fact about the thing.
Lovely is entirely your opinion, so it goes furthest away.
Wooden is a plain fact, so it sits right against the noun — so tightly that wooden table functions almost as a single word.
Size, age, shape and colour sit in between in roughly that order of increasing factuality, which is not a perfect explanation but is a workable one.
For conversation, where you cannot check eight categories, three fragments cover most cases. Opinion first. Material last. Size before colour.
And there is a way to avoid the problem entirely, which is what fluent speakers actually do most of the time: stop stacking. Instead of a small old Italian wooden table, write a small wooden table that we bought in Italy. Four stacked adjectives are grammatically correct and stylistically heavy, and breaking them into a clause is usually better writing regardless of the order rule.
So the order is worth knowing so that two or three adjectives come out right, and worth avoiding beyond that.

readings.title: Words That Are Already at the End
readings.passageScript:
Cold is a scale. You can be slightly cold, quite cold, very cold, extremely cold. There is always further to go.
Freezing is not a point on that scale. It is the end of it. Freezing does not mean cold; it means at the extreme of cold.
This is the difference between a gradable and a non-gradable adjective, and it decides which degree word you can use.
Gradable adjectives take very, quite, rather, extremely, slightly, a bit.
Non-gradable adjectives take absolutely, completely, utterly, totally, entirely.
Very cold. Absolutely freezing.
Very tired. Absolutely exhausted.
Very angry. Absolutely furious.
Very difficult. Completely impossible.
Very freezing is the most recognisable error in this whole area, and it is easy to avoid once you can spot the class. The test: does the adjective already mean extremely something? If so, it is non-gradable and very will not fit.
Two things make this easier than it looks.
Really works with both. Really cold and really freezing are both fine. When you are unsure, really is the safe choice, and it costs you nothing in accuracy.
And the pairs come in twos, so learning one gives you the other. Cold and freezing, hot and boiling, tired and exhausted, angry and furious, pleased and delighted, big and enormous, small and tiny, difficult and impossible, good and perfect, surprising and astonishing.
One warning that is about judgement rather than grammar. Non-gradable adjectives are strong, so they should be rare. Somebody who is absolutely exhausted every evening and utterly furious about every delay has spent the words, and when something genuinely extreme happens they have nothing left to say about it. Precision means keeping the strong word for the occasion that deserves it.

grammar.title: Ordering two or more adjectives
grammar.explanation: A fixed order that every English speaker follows and almost none can state. Worth knowing for two or three adjectives, and worth avoiding beyond that.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE ORDER
  opinion, size, age, shape, colour,
  origin, material, purpose

  a lovely little old rectangular brown
  Italian wooden dining table
  ^ all eight. No real sentence does this.
    Three is common. Four is heavy.

THE IDEA BEHIND IT
  far from the noun  = your VIEW
  close to the noun  = a FACT

  lovely  -> pure opinion, goes first
  wooden  -> pure fact, sits against the
             noun (wooden table is almost
             one word)

THE CONVERSATION VERSION
  opinion first
  material last
  size before colour

WHAT FLUENT SPEAKERS ACTUALLY DO
  stop stacking. Use a clause.
     a small wooden table that we
     bought in Italy
  rather than
     a small old Italian wooden table
grammar.workedExample:
You want to describe a table: it is small, it is round, and it is made of wood.
1. Sort them by category. Small is size. Round is shape. Wooden is material.
2. Put them in order: size, then shape, then material.
3. Result: a small round wooden table.
Check it with the idea behind the rule: wooden is the plainest fact, so it sits against the noun. Small is the least factual of the three, so it goes furthest away.
Now one with four. It is lovely, it is old, it is brown, and it is Italian.
1. Opinion, age, colour, origin. In order: a lovely old brown Italian table.
2. That is correct and it is heavy.
3. So do what a fluent writer would: a lovely old table, brown, that came from Italy.
Four stacked adjectives are never wrong and rarely the best choice.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting material or origin early — a wooden small table, an Italian old brown table. Material sits closest to the noun and origin is second closest, and moving either is the most audible version of this error. The other mistake is stacking four or five because the rule permits it; permitted and readable are different things.
grammar.memoryTip: Opinion first, material last, size before colour. Beyond three, use a clause.

1. a small round wooden table
2. a thick grey woollen coat
3. a tiny rectangular metal box
4. an enormous ancient stone building
5. a vivid green plastic case
6. Model: an enormous stone building, and an ancient one — or: an enormous stone building that has been there for centuries.
In every one, the material word came last: wooden, woollen, metal, stone, plastic. That is the single most reliable part of the order and worth checking first.
Number 5 is colour then material, and vivid modifies green rather than the case — vivid green is functioning as one colour word.

grammar.title: Comparative and superlative adverbs
grammar.explanation: Level 1 Unit 12 gave you adverbs of manner. These are their comparative and superlative forms, and the rule follows the adjectives from Unit 4 with one group that behaves differently.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
MOST ADVERBS END IN -LY, so they are long,
so they take MORE and THE MOST
  carefully  more carefully  the most carefully
  quickly    more quickly    the most quickly
  politely   more politely   the most politely

BUT a small group are SHORT and take -ER
  fast    faster    the fastest
  hard    harder    the hardest
  early   earlier   the earliest
  late    later     the latest
  long    longer    the longest

IRREGULARS - the same two as always
  well    better    the best
  badly   worse     the worst

THE ERRORS:
  more faster        (never both)
  more quicker       (never both)
  quicklier          (long ones take more)
  more well          (it is better)
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say somebody does something with more care than before.
1. The adverb is carefully.
2. Is it long? Yes — it ends in -ly and has three syllables.
3. Long adverbs take more: more carefully.
4. Result: She works more carefully than she used to.
Now a short one. You want to say somebody runs at greater speed.
1. The adverb is fast. Note it has no -ly at all — fast is both adjective and adverb.
2. It is short, so it takes -er: faster.
3. Result: He runs faster than me.
And the irregular: he does it well becomes he does it better, never more well. That one is worth saying aloud until it is automatic, because more well is a natural-sounding error that the rule would otherwise produce.
grammar.commonMistake: Using more with a form that already has -er — more faster, more quicker. English marks the comparative once. The other error is putting -er on a long -ly adverb, producing quicklier or carefullier, which do not exist. And more well, which the rule predicts and English rejects in favour of better.
grammar.memoryTip: Long -ly adverbs take more. Short ones take -er. Well becomes better.

grammar.title: Gradable and non-gradable adjectives
grammar.explanation: Some adjectives sit on a scale and some are already at the end of one. The two kinds take different degree words, and mixing them is the most recognisable error in this area.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
GRADABLE - a point on a scale
  cold, hot, tired, angry, big, difficult
  take: very, quite, rather, extremely,
        slightly, a bit

NON-GRADABLE - already at the END
  freezing, boiling, exhausted, furious,
  enormous, impossible
  take: absolutely, completely, utterly,
        totally, entirely

  very cold        absolutely freezing
  very tired       absolutely exhausted
  very angry       absolutely furious
  very difficult   completely impossible

  NOT very freezing.

THE TEST:
  does it already mean EXTREMELY something?
  If yes, it is non-gradable.

THE SAFE CHOICE:
  REALLY works with both.
     really cold / really freezing

THE PAIRS - learn one, get the other
  cold/freezing      hot/boiling
  tired/exhausted    angry/furious
  pleased/delighted  big/enormous
  small/tiny         difficult/impossible
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say it was extremely cold.
1. You could use the gradable word with its degree word: it was very cold.
2. Or you could use the non-gradable word: freezing. But then very will not fit.
3. Non-gradable adjectives take absolutely: it was absolutely freezing.
4. Check the test — does freezing already mean extremely cold? Yes. So it is non-gradable, and very has nowhere to add.
Now an adjective you have not met. Suppose somebody says astonishing. Is it gradable?
1. Apply the test. Does it already mean extremely surprising? Yes.
2. So it is non-gradable: absolutely astonishing, not very astonishing.
The test works on words you have never seen, which is why it is worth more than the list of pairs.
grammar.commonMistake: Very freezing, very exhausted, very impossible. This is the most audible non-native pattern in the whole area and the test fixes it in one step. The other error is the reverse — absolutely cold, absolutely tired — which sounds odd for the opposite reason: you are using a total word on something that has degrees.
grammar.memoryTip: Already at the extreme? Absolutely. On a scale? Very. Unsure? Really.

8. ____ impossible
grammar.answerKey:
1. very — G  2. absolutely — N  3. very — G  4. absolutely — N  5. very — G  6. absolutely — N  7. very — G  8. absolutely — N
They are four pairs, and in each pair the second word already contains the idea of extremely. Freezing is extremely cold; exhausted is extremely tired; furious is extremely angry; impossible is beyond difficult.
For any of these, really would also have been correct — really cold and really freezing are both fine. If you are unsure in conversation, that is the escape route.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key — they are your examples.
What most people find: two adjectives is by far the commonest, three is occasional, and four or more is rare enough that you may not find a single one in twelve examples. That is the finding — the rule has eight slots and real English uses two.
The second finding is that the material slot is the easiest to spot and the most consistently filled. If your examples contain a material word, it will be against the noun in every single case.
The labelling is harder than it looks for opinion and size, because words like great and huge can be read either way. Any example you could not label confidently is worth keeping — the ambiguous ones are where the categories are doing least work.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key.
What most people find in advertising: the strong words are almost never attached to anything checkable, and the same three or four adjectives repeat constantly. Stunning, amazing, perfect and unique do most of the work, and none of them can be measured.
In ordinary speech the pattern is different and worth noticing. People do use these words, and they use them about genuinely extreme things — absolutely exhausted after a fourteen-hour day, absolutely furious about something that deserved it. The words still carry weight there because they are rare.
That contrast is the practical lesson of this unit: the same grammar, used precisely, means something, and used constantly, means nothing.
